How to play

Grave Wounds is a roleplaying game about small bands of fighting men and women in real wars, and about what wounds do to them. There are no hit points. A wound is a place on the body, the way it was made and how bad it is, and those three things decide whether it bleeds, hurts, stops a hand gripping or a leg bearing weight, and how long it would take to kill without help. Most wounds do not kill. They stop a fighter, and then the question is whether his friends can stop the bleeding, carry him to camp and keep the fever off.

What you need

  • Dice. Everything is rolled on d100: two ten-sided dice, one for tens and one for units, 01 to 00 (00 is 100). A few rolls use a single d10.
  • The pages. The wound roller, the team builder, the travel map and the field map run on any browser and keep your game in it. They roll the dice, look up the tables and keep the count, so the table can play quickly. Everything they do is written here, and the printed tables hold every table, so the game can be played on paper too.
  • A GM and players. One person runs the world and the enemy (the GM). Each player runs a team of four to six characters, not a single hero, so losing one is a loss and not the end of the evening.

The one roll

Every test is the same: roll d100, and equal to or under the number you are rolling against succeeds. That number is a skill or a characteristic, less any penalties. How far under you rolled is the margin, and in a fight the margin matters: a hit by a wide margin is a worse wound.

The running example

This book follows one team from start to finish: a lord's retinue on the road to Towton in 1461, led by William of Ely. Each chapter picks up the story where the last left it: the team is made, Walter Miller the archer shoots and is cut down, his friends stop the bleeding, and he is carried to camp to heal or die. The numbers in the example are the game's own; where a die is rolled, the book says what came up.

Time

The game's clock changes with what the team is doing:

Scale How long For
Round 6 seconds One action in a fight; bleeding; stop checks
Minute 10 rounds Binding wounds; the end of most fights
Day Marching, camps, the weather, sickness
Week Wounds healing in camp; catching disease

Characteristics and skills

Every character has six characteristics, from 15 to 95: Strength, Agility, Endurance, Wits, Nerve and Presence. Fifty is an ordinary person. Skills (Bow, Blade, Dodge, Leechcraft and the rest) start from a characteristic and grow with experience, up to 90. A character's attack is the skill his weapon is fought with, and his defence is the better of Parry and Dodge.

Anyone without a sheet (a bystander, an enemy the GM has not written up) counts as 50 in every characteristic, and fights at his quality:

Quality Attack Defence Nerve
Green 40% 25% 35
Regular 50% 35% 50
Veteran 60% 45% 65

For the GM

Quality is the quickest way to make an enemy: decide whether he is green, regular or veteran, and the table gives his attack, defence and Nerve. The followers of the players' teams use the same table, and so do whole units on the field map.

Making a team

A team is four to six characters with a shared history: a lord's retinue, a free company, a patrol. The first character leads it, and when he falls another steps up. The team builder makes a whole team in one click, or one character at a time, from the tables of 11 eras; the printed tables hold the same tables for the table top. This chapter uses the medieval tables (c.1250–1460). The other eras follow the same five steps with their own careers, skills and kit (Other wars).

The five steps

1. Characteristics. Roll 3d6 × 5 for each characteristic in order (15 to 90), or take the fixed array 70, 60, 55, 50, 45, 35 and place it, highest first, where the character's career wants it most.

2. Origin. Roll d100 on the origin table (20 origins). It says where he comes from, gives one skill +15, and a trait and a drawback that go together: a characteristic ±10 or a skill ±15.

3. Career terms. The leader serves three terms, the others one or two. In each term:

  • his career's main skill rises, +15 in the first term and +10 after;
  • its second skill rises +5;
  • d100 on the career's table gives an event, and the skill it taught rises +15. An event he has had already moves to the next row down.

He starts at 16 and is 4 years older for each term. Nobody dies while being made. The 12 medieval careers:

Career Main skill Second skill
Man-at-arms Blade Parry
Archer Bow Dodge
Crossbowman Crossbow Dodge
Spearman or billman Polearm Parry
Mounted sergeant Ride Parry
Mercenary Axe and mace Parry
Sailor Seamanship Dodge
Clerk or priest Letters Persuade
Barber-surgeon Leechcraft Craft
Forester or huntsman Fieldcraft Stealth
Servant or groom Ride Watch
Merchant Persuade Letters

4. Old wounds. A term marked * on its table (a siege, a broken line, a rout) leaves an old wound, and so does a d100 at or under the career's wound chance. Its place is rolled on the region's own wound table, the same one the roller uses. Then d100: up to 70, a healed scar; above, a lasting hurt, 5 off the characteristic that place governs (Wits for the head, Presence for the face, Strength for the arms, Agility for the legs, Endurance for the body).

5. Skills and kit. Each skill starts at a characteristic divided by 2, 3, 4 or 5 (rounded down), plus what he gained, to 90 at most. His kit and weapon come with his first career and his region.

The retinue: Walter Miller

The team builder rolls a lord's retinue from England: William of Ely, a man-at-arms, leads it. Its senior archer is Walter Miller, 2 terms, age 24: Strength 40, Agility 65, Endurance 35, Wits 60, Nerve 50, Presence 50. He was raised on the pilgrim roads (speaks three tongues; belongs nowhere), and in his terms he scouted ahead of the army and foraged through a hungry winter. His skills that matter here: Bow 57, Dodge 31, Fieldcraft 50, Stealth 36. He fights with the longbow at 57%, and his defence is 32%.

His Endurance is low, and it shows in a fight: his Blood is 18, not the usual 20 (next chapter). With Agility 65 he rolls d10 + 6 for initiative.

Followers

A big team's other men get no sheet, only a line: a career, a name and a quality, rolled on d100. The quality gives their attack, defence and Nerve (the table in How to play). Some teams roll on a better or worse table:

Quality table Green Regular Veteran
Default 01–30 31–80 81–00
Hardened 01–15 16–60 61–00
Raw 01–55 56–90 91–00

For the GM

Followers are what make a team feel like a household or a company, and they are who dies first. Name them; the players will remember them. On the field map they fight as units around the team, who go with them as heroes.

The fight

A fight runs in rounds of 6 seconds. Each round every fighter who can act takes one turn, in order of initiative; then the round ends, the wounded bleed and the sides check their nerve. Most fights last a minute or two: one side breaks long before it is all down.

The wound roller runs all of this: pick an attacker and a defender, roll the hit, apply it, and press Next fighter and Next round. Its battle map is a grid of hexes about 2 yards (2 m) across.

A fighter's turn

  1. Initiative. At the start of the fight each fighter rolls d10 + Agility ÷ 10 (rounded down), and they act from highest to lowest. A fighter who is down, out of the fight, or on a side that has broken does not act.
  2. Move or stay. He may stay, advance up to 4 hexes and still attack, or run up to 12 hexes and not attack. He may pass through friends but not stop on them. Leaving an enemy's side by more than one step gives that enemy a free attack.
  3. Attack. Roll d100 against his attack, less his wound penalties and any range penalty. Equal or under hits, and the margin is how far under. A roll at or under a tenth of the chance is a critical: it cannot be defended.
  4. Defence. The defender may roll d100 against his defence (Parry or Dodge), less his own penalties. Equal or under, the blow misses.
  5. Where it lands. Roll d100 on the era's hit-location table for the place, and on the weapon's table for how it wounds: a cut, a thrust (pierce), a crushing blow, a bullet.
  6. How bad. The margin sets the severity: under 20 light, from 20 serious, from 50 (or on a critical) critical. Firearms have their own bands for the body and the limbs. A hit by a margin of 2 or less, if it is not a critical, only grazes: its bleeding and pain are a step less, and it calls for no stop check.
  7. Armour. The armour on that place lowers the severity a step at a time against that kind of blow, if its coverage roll says the blow met it. Some weapons are made to beat armour: a war bow's heavy arrows go through mail and a jack as if they were not there.
  8. The wound. Look up the wound for the place, the kind of blow and the severity, and write it down. Its effects are in the next chapter.
  9. The stop check. A serious and critical wound that carries shock (most do; many limb wounds do not) calls for a d100 against the wounded man's Nerve, less his pain and blood-loss penalties, and 10 more for a critical wound:
Result He is Which means
Equal or under Fighting on No change
Failed by 1–20 Defend only for 2 rounds No attack; he may move and defend
Failed by 21–40 Stunned for 2 rounds No attack; −50% to his defence
Failed by more than 40 Out of the fight until helped or the fight ends Takes no part: no attack, no defence

A worse result replaces a milder one, and the round it happens in is the first of its rounds. This is what ends real fights: men stop, sit down, crawl away, long before they die.

The retinue: the arrow

On the road to Towton the retinue meets a band of Lancastrian billmen, regulars. It is Walter Miller's turn, and the nearest billman is in short range. He shoots at 57% and rolls 21: a hit by a margin of 36, serious. The billman tries to dodge at 35% and rolls 61: no. The arrow strikes his chest (left), a thrust. His jack would take the wound down 1 step, but the war bow's arrows ignore it, so it stays serious: bleeding 2, pain 2, short of breath, and it would kill in hours untreated. It carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 50, less 2 steps of pain, gives 30. He rolls 47, failing by 17: he can defend only for 2 rounds.

The retinue: the bill

The billmen close. One reaches Walter and swings at 50%, rolling 22: a margin of 28, serious. Walter dodges at 32% and rolls 58. The bill opens his thigh (right), a cut, where his jack does not reach. The wound bleeds 3 (arterial), pain 2, and the leg is hurt. It does not carry shock, so there is no stop check, and he fights on. But at 3 Blood a round, his 18 Blood will be gone in 6 rounds. The next chapter is about what that means.

The end of the round

  • Bleeding. Every wounded fighter loses Blood at his wounds' rate (next chapter).
  • Results wear off. Defend only and stunned count down a round.
  • Pain. A fighter whose pain is above the cap (3 steps, −30%) makes a stop check every round, as for a serious wound.
  • Morale. A side with 25% or more of its fighters down rolls d100 against the best Nerve among those still up (its leader's, if he is up): +10 while a leader is up, and (Presence − 50) ÷ 5 more for him; −20 if a leader is down; −20 once 50% of the side is down. Over the target, the side breaks: it runs or surrenders.

For the GM

The roller asks for the stop check and the morale roll when they are due, and you can type your own dice into it. Remember that most enemies want to live too: a side that breaks runs, and a man who is down asks for quarter. A fight is usually decided in a minute.

Wounds and movement

A leg wound halves a fighter's move (advance 2, run 6). A man who has collapsed or cannot stand crawls 1 hex. A winded man cannot run, and a stunned or out man cannot move at all. The printed tables and the roller's battle map have the rest: ground, height, cover, works and weather.

Wounds

A wound is written down as what it does. Each one has five things, and they add up across all of a fighter's wounds:

  • Bleeding, from B0 (none) to B3 (arterial).
  • Pain, from P0 to P3.
  • Impairments: what the wound stops the body doing.
  • Shock, fracture or severed: shock calls for the stop check; a fracture is a bone that needs setting; a severed part is gone.
  • The clock: how long it would take to kill him untreated, from none through days, hours, minutes and rounds to instant.

Blood

Every fighter has a Blood pool: 20, plus (Endurance − 50) ÷ 10, rounded down (16 at Endurance 15, 24 at 95). Each wound bleeds away Blood at its rate:

Bleed Blood lost What it is
B0 none None
B1 1 a minute Slow: seeping; lose 1 Blood per minute
B2 1 a round Heavy: lose 1 Blood per round; bind within minutes
B3 3 a round Arterial: lose 3 Blood per round; tourniquet or pressure now

As Blood falls, so does the fighter:

Blood left Effect
75% or less Pale and weak: -10% to all actions
50% or less Faint check each minute; -20% to all actions
25% or less Barely conscious: -40% to all actions, can only crawl
None Unconscious and dying

Bleeding is what kills quickly. A man with an arterial wound has a few rounds; a man with a heavy one has a few minutes; slow bleeding gives his friends time.

Penalties

A wounded fighter fights worse. Add up:

  • Pain: −10% to attack and defence for each step, counted to 3 steps at most (and above that, a stop check every round).
  • Blood lost: the table above.
  • Impairments, each counted once however many wounds cause it. An arm's impairment counts against his weapon arm (his weapon hand's side) or his shield arm (the other):
Impairment What it does Attack Defence
Dazed Stunned: lose next action, then -20% for 1d6 rounds −20% −20%
Vision Vision impaired: -30% to sight-based actions; blinded if both eyes −30% −30%
Breath Winded: no sustained exertion; fatigue doubled −10% −10%
Collapse Collapses; can only crawl or crouch −20% −30%
Stand Falls and cannot stand unaided −20% −30%
Leg Movement halved; -20% to footwork and dodging — −20%
Move Movement halved — −10%
Unconscious Knocked out (check each minute to wake) — —
Speech Cannot speak clearly — —
Arm (weapon arm) That arm -20%; no two-handed use −20% —
Arm (shield arm) That arm -20%; no two-handed use — −10%
Grip (weapon arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it −30% —
Grip (shield arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it — —
Hand useless (weapon arm) That hand useless −30% —
Hand useless (shield arm) That hand useless — —
Arm useless (weapon arm) That arm useless −40% —
Arm useless (shield arm) That arm useless — −10%

Attack and defence penalties are each capped at −60%. A fighter with no usable hand cannot hold a weapon. A fighter with either arm hurt (an arm wound, a lost grip, a useless hand or arm) cannot attack with a two-handed weapon (bows, crossbows, long guns, bills, pikes and poleaxes): he can only defend until he takes up something he can use in one hand.

First aid

A wound can be treated three ways (on the roller, the buttons on the casualty's card). How long it takes, and whether anyone can reach him under fire, is the GM's call:

  • Bind: pressure and a bandage, one step less bleeding.
  • Tourniquet: an arm or a leg only; the bleeding stops. Left on for hours, the limb is lost.
  • Cauterise: the bleeding stops, at one more step of pain.

If anyone on his side comes from the team builder, the best Leechcraft among them still standing rolls d100 for each treatment. Success: a bind stops 2 steps instead of one, and cautery adds no pain. Failure: nothing happens, and it can be tried again next turn. A side with no sheets binds without rolling.

The retinue: the tourniquet

Walter's thigh bleeds 3 Blood a round. The best Leechcraft in the retinue is not its barber-surgeon's but Geoffrey Cooper's, the servant or groom: 27. He drags Walter back and tries a tourniquet; he rolls 41, over his 27, and the strap slips. He tries again the next round and rolls 19: it holds, and the bleeding stops. Two rounds of bleeding have left Walter 12 of 18 Blood: pale and weak.

His wound penalties now: pain 2 and the Blood he lost give −30% to attack; his hurt leg adds to his defence, −50%. He moves at half pace. He is out of this fight in all but name, and alive.

For the GM

The clock is a guide to the story, not a timer to run down: a wound fatal in hours is one that needs a surgeon tonight, not one that kills on the stroke of the hour. Blood is what the rules count. A man who reaches no Blood is unconscious and dying; what happens next is first aid, luck, and the camp.

Recovery

After the fight come the days that decide who lives. Wounds, sickness and fever all move on one track of five steps, and each step weakens a man in the next fight:

Step In a fight
Healed —
Mending −10% to attack and defence
Serious −25% to attack and defence, cannot run
Grave −25% to attack and defence, crawls only, defends only
Deadly too ill to fight

Into camp

Each wound goes onto the track at the step its severity gives (light mending, serious serious, critical grave), or worse if its clock is short: a wound that would kill in hours or minutes starts at grave. In camp the bleeding stops, and each night he gets back 4 Blood.

On the wound roller, put him With his force on the travel map and press To camp; the travel map's nights then run his wounds with the force's own wounded.

The recovery check

Once every 7 days, each wound makes a recovery check: d100 against his Endurance, adjusted:

What To the roll
Care: no camp -20
Care: a camp +0
Care: quarters in houses +10
He marched that day -20
He rested +10
A night harder than the shelter (cold, wet) -10
Poor hygiene -10
A leech with the force + his Leechcraft ÷ 10
Battle wounds heal easily +20
Wound fever is hard −25
  • Succeed by 30 or more: two steps better.
  • Succeed: one step better.
  • Fail: it holds; at deadly, he dies.
  • Fail by 30 or more: one step worse.

A wound that reaches healed leaves a scar on his sheet and figure.

Wound fever

3 to 5 days after the fight, each wound turns septic or it does not: 5% for a wound with a low risk of infection, 15% medium, 30% high; +5 with no camp, −5 in quarters, less a leech's bonus. A septic wound is wound fever: a step worse, checked every night, and the check is harder by 25. Before antibiotics, this is what killed the men who survived the battle.

The retinue: the camp

The retinue carries Walter to its camp. His wound goes onto the track at serious. A few nights on, its risk of fever is 13% (medium, less 2 for Geoffrey Cooper's Leechcraft). The GM rolls 64: it stays clean.

At the end of the week he checks: Endurance 35, a camp (+0), resting (+10), a leech (+2) and a battle wound (+20) make 67. He rolls 52, a success by 15: one step better, mending. A week later he rolls 30, a success by 37: healed, with a scar on his right thigh. His Blood came back in his first nights in camp, and the retinue marches on with its archer.

For the GM

The track is where the campaign's hard choices are made. March on, and every check is -20; camp in the open, and fever is likelier; stay in a filthy camp, and the flux comes. The travel map counts all of it for whole forces; the players only have to decide.

Battles of hundreds

When hundreds fight, rolling for every man every round would take all night. On the field map the rank and file fight as units, resolved a minute at a time through the same wound tables, and the team fights among them as heroes with the full rules of the fight.

The field map

The field map is a grid of hexes 11 yards (10 m) across. One exchange is about a minute, some 10 rounds. Each exchange, one side moves, then the other, and then every melee and volley is resolved at once.

A unit is a block of hexes: its front row along its line, its men in rows behind. It has a number of men, a quality (green, regular or veteran, as in How to play), a weapon, armour and a formation:

Formation Men a hex Abreast Ranks Move (hexes) Shots at it count
Close order 40 10 4 6 ×1
Open order 20 10 2 8 ×0.8
Battery 20 4 5 6 ×0.8
Extended order 3 3 1 8 ×0.5
Machine-gun team 5 5 1 4 ×0.5
Anti-tank guns 5 1 1 2 ×0.5

Mounted units move 15 hexes. A unit that ends its move touching the enemy may have come up to 2 times its move: a charge. A unit in contact cannot move. Units cannot pass through each other, except that a steady unit charging may pass through its own side's men to reach the enemy; the units it passes through lose half their move that exchange.

Seeing. To aim, to lay a gun on a target or to call fire, a man must see it. Woods and buildings between block his sight unless they stand lower than he does; he sees 1 hex into them, and out of them from their edge. Ground between that stands higher than both him and his target is dead ground: a rise hides each from the other. A crest within 1 hex of either man does not count, so a man or a tank pulled up just behind it sees over it and is seen, and a man on the top sees down both slopes.

An exchange

  1. Who strikes. In melee, the front rank of each hex touching the enemy, and one more rank for each hex of the weapon's reach past the first (spears and bills strike from two ranks, the pike from three). With missiles, the men who have the target in range.
  2. How many blows tell. Most of a minute in a press is shoving and watching for an opening: about one striking man in 11 makes a real attempt each exchange. A longbowman looses 8 arrows a minute, and about one shot in 30 is aimed at a man rather than loosed at the mass.
  3. Each attempt is one attack, at the unit's quality, exactly as in the fight: +20 from the flank, +30 from the rear (and no parry), +20 for a mounted charge in its first exchange, −10 for a shaken unit, +20 for pikes in close order against horse to their front; range, weather and cover come off missiles. A tired unit loses its fatigue level's penalty off its attack and its parry.
  4. The wound is rolled as for one man. A light wound or a graze: he fights on. Serious or critical: a stop check, and failing it puts him down. A wound that kills within rounds kills. Against modern fire (breech-loaders on, machine guns, shell, grenades), every serious or critical wound puts him down and a light one calls for the check: the casualty returns from 1914 on count nearly every man hit as out of the line.
  5. Morale, below; then the next exchange.

Fatigue. A unit tires as a character does. Each exchange it fights hand to hand counts one toil, and so does each hex it goes in deep mud or snow. After 12 toil in heavy armour, 20 in medium, or 30 in light, it is a fatigue step worse, to Exhausted at most, and stays so for the battle. Shooting costs none, and vehicles don't tire.

Quick-play blows (a GM's choice). Rolling every blow is exact but slow on a table. To roll a group's blows in one go: count the tries as above, then find the men down per 100 tries in the era's quick-play chart (in the tables) for the weapon against the target's armour, at the attack after all modifiers, times the quality factor printed with it, times (1 − parry × 0.9) if the target can parry. Tries × that ÷ 100 is the average; roll d100 on the spread chart for the men down. The field page's Quick-play sheet prints the exact figures for the units on the field, and ticking quick-play blows makes the page roll this way too. Blows that fall on a hero are still rolled one at a time. It gives the same losses on average, with the same spread, as rolling every blow. Shellfire goes the same way (see fire support): one roll for one battery's fire on one unit.

Morale and the rout

After an exchange a unit checks its morale if it lost the exchange in contact (more of its men down than it put down), has 25% of its men down, lost 10% of its men in this exchange, or was struck in the flank or rear. It rolls d100 against its quality's Nerve:

Modifier
Still steady, ranks closed +20
A named leader with it, up +10
Its leader down −20
Half its men down −20
Struck in flank or rear −20
A steady friendly unit beside it +10
Dug in: gone to ground or in a bunker +10
Lost the exchange −5 a man more lost than it put down (at most −30)
  • Steady, fails: it is shaken: it fights at −10 and cannot charge. Failing by more than 20 while flanked, or with half its men down, it breaks at once.
  • Shaken, fails: it breaks.
  • Shaken, passes out of contact: it rallies to steady.

A broken unit runs. Every enemy man in reach strikes it at +20, with no parry and twice as often, as long as the pursuers keep up. This is where most of a battle's dead fell, as at Towton and Agincourt, where the beaten side lost far more men in flight than in the press.

On the field map it runs straight back as far as it can move. Its own side's units do not stop it: it runs on through them to the first clear ground beyond, and each unit it runs through loses half its move that exchange as the fugitives push through its ranks.

For the GM

A melee of ten or twenty minutes, decided by morale more than by wounds, with the beaten side losing most of its men in the rout: that is the shape the records show, and the page is tuned to give it. Let the players' heroes break a line rather than kill it.

Ammunition

A unit that shoots carries only so much. Its load is counted in exchanges of fire: the rounds, arrows or bolts a man carries (a machine gun's belts, for a gun), over the rate it fires at, times 30% (men do not fire every round they could). Longbowmen have about 20 exchanges of shooting, riflemen of 1914-53 about 40, a machine gun about 22. Vehicles and guns count their own rounds.

  • Running low. Each exchange it shoots uses one. At 25% of a full load or less it shoots at half rate; with none it cannot shoot at all, still fights hand to hand, and has -10 on morale.
  • Resupply. An exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing, within 5 hexes of a supply source: its side's map edge (behind the way most of its men face), a lorry or armoured carrier of its side, or a supply dump. The GM places dumps before the battle; from the Second World War on, an air drop called on a side's move lands as a dump at the end of the exchange, a little off the mark, and from Vietnam on a helicopter can set one down on a landing zone (Landing by air).
  • The enemy commander resupplies a unit that is out, or low with no enemy in its range, when a source is in reach. Attacking, a unit out of ammunition with none in reach falls back toward its edge; holding, it stays and fights hand to hand.

Heroes

A team's characters go with units as heroes: in the front rank, shooting with it, or behind it. A hero in the front makes 3 times a ranker's attempts with his own attack, and blows on his unit's front fall on him 2 times as often as on a ranker there. His wounds use the full rules, his own Blood and his own stop check. Two front-rank heroes in contact fight each other: 3 attempts each an exchange, instead of at the rankers.

His wounds slow him as in Wounds: an arm hurt stops a two-handed weapon, and a lamed hero halves his unit's move. In a quiet exchange his friends give first aid: the best Leechcraft in the unit, or its medics, else his comrades at 60%. A lamed or down hero can be carried back by 2 of his unit's men, or left behind. A wounded hero who can still walk can go back alone. Where he goes depends on whether his side has an aid post:

  • With an aid post (the GM places one for each side), the party crosses the map 3 hexes an exchange on open ground by the cheapest way (round water, walls and the enemy, slower through woods), and shells can catch it on the way. At the post he gets first aid every exchange at 75%, and his wounds come off the death clock. An enemy who reaches the post takes or kills the men there. On its side's move the GM can move the post; the men there go with it, and it gives no first aid that exchange.
  • With none, he is carried off the map at once, and the bearers return after 3 exchanges.

A hero left behind lies on his unit's hex. A unit of his side that stands there picks him up; an enemy unit takes him prisoner or kills him, by the war's custom of quarter. When the battle ends, a hero still lying out there is found if his side holds the field; if not, quarter decides.

The retinue: at Towton

On the field map the retinue's followers fight as units: its archers in open order, its spearmen in close order. William of Ely goes with the spearmen in the front rank; Walter Miller shoots with the archers, at his own 57% rather than the unit's quality, and makes 3 times as many aimed shots as one of them. When the billmen close, blows on the archers' front can find him, and a wound there is his own: rolled in full, bled on his own 18 Blood, and carried back to the roller when the battle is over.

The enemy commander

The GM can hand one side to a scripted enemy commander, attacking or holding. At the start of that side's move it orders each unit. It knows only the enemies its units can see (or saw in the last 3 exchanges, where they were then; what a unit sees from where it has just moved, the units ordered after it know); green units go for the nearest, better ones for an enemy that is hurt, shaken or dangerous to them. It closes, takes cover, shoots from range or charges with the odds its quality wants (counting the steady friends touching it, who go in with it), and green units sometimes hesitate. With no enemy in sight, a unit holds; attacking with no objective, it goes forward along its facing to find one. A unit with no room to move facing its goal (or a turn too dear) moves facing as near its goal as it can.

  • Storming works. Attacking, infantry with muskets, rifle-muskets, breech-loaders, or modern rifles and sub-machine guns do not stop to trade fire with an enemy behind works (a parapet, trench or bank), dug in, or in buildings or rubble: they close without seeking cover, firing as they go, and charge it, with the same odds. Flintlock riflemen, archers and machine guns still fight by fire. Modern infantry storm in bounds: a unit that took fire in the last exchange goes to ground and fires this move, and goes on once a bound draws no fire, its target is pinned, or it can charge home. A wall or palisade that blocks hand-to-hand fighting stops them at its foot, unless they carry ladders: then they go up it (see works). Breaching it is the GM's order.

  • Routes. A battlefield can send a unit on a route round a flank, as its account tells: the commander moves it from waypoint to waypoint, turning aside only for an enemy in contact or across its way, then orders it as any other.

  • Orders from the accounts. On the battlefields, units that the sources say held their ground fight where they stand rather than fall back, and units the sources say withdrew on orders fall back at the minute the accounts give, to a place or off the field.
  • Narrowing. Attacking, a formed unit that the ground keeps from closing on its target closes in its front, a quarter at a time and deeper, until it can move nearer, but never to less than half the front it started with.
  • Pursuit. Its horse ride down a broken enemy within a charge when no standing enemy is as near, and its foot go after one within their move that is nearer than any standing enemy. Veterans rally back to the fight after a couple of moves if the enemy still stands near.
  • Shooters give way. Attacking, archers, crossbowmen and skirmishers in open order step aside when they stand in the way of their own formed men behind them, and the formed men go on.
  • In range means the weapon reaches, the light lets it see, and nothing blocks the line from where it would stand.
  • Tanks. A unit with a main gun counts the target in range where the gun reaches and it can see; a vehicle with one prefers a spot where the target can neither reach it nor see it.
  • Reserve. Regulars and veterans hold back their rearmost units (not one on a route, nor tanks and other vehicles with a main gun), and commit one when a unit of theirs breaks or the enemy comes close; veterans also commit to exploit an enemy rout. Attacking, they also commit one when the attack has stalled: five moves without putting down any real share of the enemy or getting nearer. A unit committed because one broke goes to plug the gap where it stood. The GM can mark reserves instead.
  • Digging in. Its foot units with modern weapons dig in where they stand when it is safe (not under fire, no enemy it knows of in their range): at the objective, holding with no objective, and in reserve while they wait.
  • Objective. The GM can mark a hex as its objective. Attacking, its units advance on it when they have nothing better to do and hold it once there (within 1 hex); holding, units more than 3 hexes from it fall back to it. Enemies near it make better targets. The log says who holds it after each exchange. Most battlefields mark the place their battle was fought for, a hill, a bridge, an outpost, as theirs, taking in the whole position (a ring of trenches counts as the hill). The GM can also mark a second objective. Attacking, once it holds the first, the units on it stay and the rest go on to the second (and back to the first if the enemy retakes it); holding, once the enemy holds the first, its units fall back to the second.
  • Minefields. It steers round minefields it knows of. Its sappers, attacking, lift a lane through known enemy mines in the row ahead when those mines lie on the way to their target or the objective, closing up to the belt first and working through it row by row. Holding, or at the objective, with no enemy it knows of within 8 hexes, they lay mines in the row ahead: mixed if the enemy it knows of has vehicles, otherwise anti-personnel.
  • Guns. It turns its guns to face the enemy and calls its off-map batteries and its aircraft (when they can fly; a strafing run or napalm strip along a wide enemy front) on what it sees, first what its forward air controllers see, and closer to its own men there. A controller with nothing to do and no target in its sight moves up to where it sees one (attacking only), up to 3 moves away, a move at a time, preferring a spot out of the enemy's reach; not while it has a fight of its own (an enemy touching it or in its own reach, pinned, or men lost the exchange before). Attacking, one battery lays a creeping barrage ahead of a unit closing on the enemy. Its batteries under counter-battery fire displace (a placed one moves its place 30 hexes along its map edge, away from the battery firing). In the dark it first has one battery fire illumination over the enemy it has lost sight of nearest its men, where it was last seen. Attacking, guns with no enemy in reach go forward: a battery limbers, moves and unlimbers once an enemy is in reach; anti-tank guns hook up to an empty tractor beside them (an empty tractor drives over to fetch them), are towed, and are unhooked in reach. They stop in reach but no nearer than 2 hexes. Holding, its guns unlimber or unhook where they stand. Attacking, its foot units get aboard empty carriers beside them while no known enemy is in reach, and get down once one is (or at the objective). Attacking or holding, guns an enemy could reach at a charge, with no steady friend on the line between, limber or hook up and pull back as far as they can from it. Attacking, it first has one battery smoke an enemy that is shooting at men who cannot reply (not in the dark, or in a gale). Then one battery fires counter-battery on a located enemy battery it can reach: the one with the best counter % on the one with the most guns still served.

Undo its orders puts the move back for the GM to make by hand.

Both sides. Each side has its own choice: moved by the GM, or the commander attacking or holding. With the commander on both sides the GM only watches: Next steps a move at a time, and Run plays on until the GM presses Stop or the run ends itself. It ends when a side has no unit left standing and none still to come, when an attacking side has taken the objective and held it 5 exchanges running with no enemy standing within 109 yards (100 m) of it and none still to come (but not before the battlefield's last phase has begun), or after 60 exchanges (on a battlefield with phases, 30 past the last phase's start, if later, but never more than 1200); then the battle ends, as with End the battle. On a battlefield the side its objective names attacks and the other holds, or the armies fight as the battlefield says they did (the choice marked as fought); on open ground both attack. The GM can take either side back at any time.

The narrative. Under the map, the page tells the battle's turning points as they happen: a phase beginning (and who comes on), units breaking or fleeing, a reserve committed, the objective taken or lost, and the end with each side's losses. With an API key of the player's own, a language model retells each one in a short passage of at most 70 words, in a voice for the war (a chronicle, a dispatch, a war diary or a situation report), or one the GM picks for the battle (any of those, a soldier's account or a plain summary). It is told to use only the facts the game gives it and to write original prose; the plain line stays under each passage. The rules never depend on it.

After the battle

End the battle stops it. The page then sets the two sides' results side by side, and says who holds the field and the objective. Then:

  1. The field. A side with no unit still standing has lost the field: the men it had down there are left behind.
  2. The death clock. A wound that kills in minutes kills before help comes, unless he is bound in time (10%). One that kills in hours kills unless his camp can treat it: 40% saved in a camp, 60% in quarters, none with no camp. Medevac does better where a side had it: ambulance wagons (the Civil War and the Indian Wars) save 50%, motor ambulances (the world wars) 65%, and helicopters (Korea on) 85%, and 20% of those dying within minutes. Helicopters need a landing zone on the field and a helicopter of the side not lost, or it is motor ambulances; the GM can untick a side that had none.
  3. To camp. The rest are carried to their force's camp and go onto the track, as in Recovery. A battle set up from the travel map sends its dead and wounded back to the forces there.

The march and the camp

Between battles the team marches, camps and sickens. The travel map moves forces across a map of hexes, usually 0.6 mile (1 km) across, on one clock for everyone.

Marching

A force marches at its kind's road speed:

Force Road speed A day on the road
On foot 2.5 mph (4 km/h) 20 miles (32 km)
Mounted 3.7 mph (6 km/h) 30 miles (48 km)
Baggage wagons 1.9 mph (3 km/h) 15 miles (24 km)

Other ground takes longer; a step from one hex to the next costs the average of the two:

Terrain Time against a road
Road ×1
Open ground ×1.5
Farmland ×1.5
Heath ×1.75
Forest ×2.5
Hills ×2
Mountains ×4
Marsh ×3
River cannot enter
Ford ×2
Bridge ×1
Lake or sea cannot enter
Village ×1
Town ×1

The march starts 1 hour after sunrise and stops 1 hour before sunset, up to 8 hours a day: a short winter day is a short march. Mud and snow slow it (next chapter), and a flooded ford cannot be crossed. These speeds are for a small, fit band; a large army's column made less ground a day.

The clock. Every force on a map keeps the same time, and it moves on only when the GM moves it: an hour, to nightfall, or until something happens. Orders say whether a force marches on its route or halts. When forces of different sides come within 1 hex of each other, the clock stops and both halt: the fight can be set up, on the roller's battle map or the field map, or they can be given new orders.

Camps

At the end of the march a force makes camp:

Camp What it is Needs Surprise Rest
Bivouac Sleep where you stop. Nothing built and no proper watch. — +20 poor
Watched camp A cleared site with fires, the baggage drawn up and a sentry roster. — 0 fair
Staked camp A watched camp ringed with sharpened stakes, like archers' stakes set against horse. tools −10 fair
Fortified camp Ditch, bank and palisade all round, with a gate. tools −20 good
Quartered Billeted in the houses of a village or town. village, town 0 good

Digging takes the work of the camp's ditches, banks, palisades and stakes, laid out as the battle map would lay them, divided among the men (75% of them work at once; the rest guard and cook). Camp work can use what is left of the marching day and then 4 evening hours; beyond that it runs on into the next day.

Surprise. When a fight is set up from the travel map, the defenders may be caught unawares: 30%, plus the camp's figure above (10 more with no camp at all), +20 in the dark, +20 in fog, plus the attackers' best Stealth ÷ 5, less the defenders' best Watch ÷ 5, and never under 5% or over 95%. Surprised men cannot attack or move in the first round.

Sickness

Before antibiotics, disease emptied armies faster than battle. Once a week every well man may catch what the camp breeds, at a chance set by its hygiene (a bivouac is poor, quarters good, other camps fair), by staying four weeks or more in one place, by the ground (marsh, a town) and by the week's weather:

Disease Caught from Shows after Deaths per case (records)
Bloody flux Dirty water or food, latrines too near the water 1–3 days 2.6%
Camp fever (typhus) Lice in crowded, unwashed camps 7–14 days 40%
Typhoid Dirty water or food, often from a carrier in camp 7–21 days 36%
Ague (malaria) Mosquitoes in marshes and low wetlands 7–28 days 0.8%
Plague Flea bites; worst in sieges and towns full of rats 2–6 days 45%

A case climbs to its peak after it shows, then gets better or worse each night on the track of Recovery, with rest, a camp and shelter helping, and marching, cold wet nights and filth hurting. Survivors of typhus and plague cannot catch it again; ague comes back in marsh country.

  • What it costs. Men at serious or worse cannot dig, fight or march on their own; at grave or worse they are carried on litters. A force carrying litters marches at 90%, or 50% with fewer than 2 fit men a litter.
  • Scurvy. After 6 weeks without fresh food (fruit, greens, fresh meat, onions), each week every well man may fall ill: 10% the first week, 10 more each week after, against his Endurance. Fresh food heals it 2 steps a week. A scurvied man's old wounds open again.
  • Frostbite. On a night of 5 °F (-15 °C) or colder, men without enough shelter may be frostbitten, a sickness on the same track.

The retinue: on the road

The retinue marches north on foot: 20 miles (32 km) a day on the road when the days are long, less in March, when Towton was fought, and less again in the snow that fell that day. It makes a watched camp each night, with a sentry roster and fires; no tools are needed. In a fair camp, moving on every day, the flux is the only real danger; were it to sit in a filthy siege camp for a month, typhus would come for it.

For the GM

The travel map counts all of this for whole forces, and runs each named character's own case with his own Endurance when you put him With a force from the roller. Your job is the choices: how hard to march, where to camp, whether to wait for the sick.

Weather, light and works

The day's weather

Each day on the travel map rolls its weather from the climate's figures for the month: its highs and lows, its days of rain and fog, its winds. Wet and dry spells last, and a warm or cold spell carries over. Rain falls as snow when the day's high is 36 °F (2 °C) or less. The GM can roll again or set any of it by hand. A sandstorm is never rolled: a battlefield names it (73 Easting, 1991) or the GM sets it.

Mud and snow build up and wear off day by day. On the travel map they slow the going; on the battle map, mud or snow at level 2 or more costs one more hex of movement every hex. Heavy rain or a storm floods the fords for 2 days, counting that day.

Weather in a fight

Weather affects missiles, never close combat:

Weather Can aim to Bows and crossbows
Fair no limit —
Overcast no limit —
Fog 55 yards (50 m) —
Rain 328 yards (300 m) −10%
Heavy rain 164 yards (150 m) −20%
Storm 109 yards (100 m) −20%
Snow 164 yards (150 m) −10%
Heavy snow 87 yards (80 m) −10%
Blizzard 33 yards (30 m) −20%
Sandstorm 437 yards (400 m) —
Wind Bows, slings, thrown Firearms Range bands with or into it
Calm or light air — — —
Breeze — — ±10%
Strong wind −10% — ±20%
Gale −20% −10% ±30%

Shooting with the wind lengthens the range bands of bows, crossbows, slings and thrown weapons; shooting into it shortens them, and rain or snow in a shooter's face halves how far he can see to aim. In the wet, a firearm can misfire, losing the shot:

Ignition Rain or snow Heavy rain, storm, blizzard
Match 30% 60%
Wheel 15% 30%
Flint 15% 30%
Percussion 5% 10%
Cartridge — —

Fatigue

A hard march, heat or cold, deep going, a bad night and hand-to-hand fighting tire a character a step at a time; a good night's rest takes it back. On the field map whole units tire the same way, from hand-to-hand fighting and deep going (an exchange):

Fatigue Attack and defence Marching speed
Fresh — 100%
Tired −5% 100%
Weary −10% 90%
Exhausted −20% 75%
Spent −30% 0%

Light

In the dark no one can see to aim, or to call fire, past the light's reach, and aimed fire is harder. A battlefield can change the light as its battle goes on, at sunset or dawn. A flare or an illumination round lights its hexes as by day for a few exchanges, and night-vision devices of the later wars see further:

Light Can see to aim Aimed fire
Daylight no limit —
Dusk or dawn 219 yards (200 m) −5%
Moonlit night 109 yards (100 m) −10%
Dark night 55 yards (50 m) −20%

Works

Camps and battlefields have works: along a hex's sides (ditches, banks, palisades, gates, walls) or in a hex (stakes, felled trees, wagons, trenches, bunkers):

Work Cover Crossing Blocks close combat
Ditch — +2 movement —
Earth bank −20% +1 movement —
Palisade −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) yes
Gate −40% free yes
Stone wall −50% cannot be crossed (breach it) yes
Stakes — +1 movement —
Abatis −20% +2 movement —
Pavise −20% free —
Wagon −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) —
Barbed wire — +3 movement —
Bunker −50% +1 movement —
Trench −40% +1 movement —
Downed helicopter −30% +2 movement —

A palisade, wall, barred gate or wagon must be breached to get through: men hack at it instead of fighting, until it is down. Across a palisade, wall or barred gate only reach-2 weapons strike, from the front rank, and striking up a bank or ditch costs its height. Horses cannot charge into stakes or felled trees.

On the field map, men on foot the GM marks with ladders can escalade a palisade, wall or barred gate instead: a few men a hex fight from the ladders at −20%, the defenders strike back at them, and once the far side is clear the unit can climb over at a cost of 4 hexes of movement.

For the GM

Weather is the cheapest way to change a fight. Rain on the morning of a battle takes the archers' edge away and spoils matchlocks; fog lets the attackers close unseen; a gale at the archers' backs carries their arrows nearly a third further. Roll it, then let the players decide whether to fight in it.

Other wars

Everything so far has used the medieval tables. The same rules carry a team through 10 more eras, from the Thirty Years' War to Afghanistan. Each era has its own skills, origins, careers, events, armies, teams and followers. Pick one with Era in the team builder.

The eras

Era Armies Fighting skills Careers A term
Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) The Swedish army (Swedes, Finns, Scots and Germans), The Imperial army and the Catholic League Musket, Pistol, Blade, Pike 9 4 years
Horse and musket (1775-1815) The Continental Army (1775-1783), The British Army in America (1775-1783), The British in the Peninsula (1808-1814), The French Empire in Spain (1808-1814), The United States (1812-1815) Musket, Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 10 4 years
Crimean War (1854-1856) British, French, Russian Musket, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 10 4 years
Plains nations (1860-1877) The Lakota (Oglala, Minneconjou and other bands), The Cheyenne and Arapaho Bow, Lance, Club and knife, Gun 7 4 years
Civil War and frontier (1861-1876) The Union (1861-1865), The Confederacy (1861-1865), The US Army on the frontier (1866-1876) Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 9 4 years
First World War (1914-1918) The British Empire, France, Germany, The United States (1917-1918) Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Bombing, Gunnery, Bayonet, Trench weapons 10 1 year
Second World War (1939-1945) The United States in Europe, US Marines and Army in the Pacific, The British Commonwealth, Germany, The Soviet Union, Japan Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 11 1 year
Korean War (1950-1953) US 1950-51, US 1952-53, Commonwealth, ROK, Chinese, North Korea Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 11 1 year
Vietnam War (1965-1973) US Army, US Marines, ANZAC, ARVN, North Vietnam, Viet Cong Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade and rocket, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 11 1 year
The Falklands to Afghanistan (1982-2014) UK 1982, Argentina 1982, US 1991, US 1993, Russia 1995, Chechens, US 2003-14, UK 2003-14, Insurgents Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Grenade and rocket, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 11 1 year

Brawl, Parry and Dodge carry over to every era, and so do the skills used outside a fight (Leechcraft, Fieldcraft, Watch, Stealth and the rest). Bow, Crossbow, Axe and Sling stay medieval (the Plains nations have their own Bow). Gunnery is the skill of men who serve guns, mortars (and, in the Crimea, of sailors serving ships' guns ashore) and, in Korea, rocket launchers and recoilless rifles. In the Crimea one Musket skill covers both the smoothbore musket and the rifle-musket. From Vietnam on, the RPG is fired with Grenade and rocket.

What changes

  • A term. Before 1914 a career term is 4 years, as in the medieval tables. From the First World War on, a term is 1 year of the war, so a soldier of three terms is about twenty-one.
  • Wound tables. Each army rolls on its own war's wound table, both for old wounds when a character is made and in the roller. Where a war's records have no wounds of some kind, the table borrows the nearest one: the pike is rolled as a long spear, and the frontier's gunshots come from the Civil War table.
  • Armour. It follows the army and the year:
  • pikemen's and cuirassiers' armours in the 1630s;
  • the steel helmet from 1915–16;
  • nylon flak vests in Korea and Vietnam;
  • plate armour in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Many armies wore none. A vest's rating against each threat (fragments, pistol rounds, rifle rounds) decides how many steps it takes off a wound, so a vest that stops a grenade fragment may do nothing against a rifle bullet. The roller and the field map read the same kits. - Kit and weapons come with the career and the army: a Viet Cong RPG gunner carries an RPG, a Second World War tank crewman a submachine gun. - Names are common names of the period and place, put together at random, and are not meant to name anyone. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese names are written family name first.

Women under arms

Where the records show women serving in a career, the team builder can roll a woman for it at that army's share. In every other army a career rolls a man, and the page gives the reason, since nurses and auxiliaries served but not in these careers. Each share is the women among the army's soldiers as a whole, not just in that career, so treat it as a rough guide. A GM may prefer to choose.

Army Share Careers open to women
Crimean War: French chosen, never rolled cantinière or canteen-keeper
Civil War and frontier: The Union (1861-1865) 0.02% infantryman, sharpshooter or skirmisher, cavalry trooper, artilleryman, scout, teamster or packer
Civil War and frontier: The Confederacy (1861-1865) 0.03% infantryman, sharpshooter or skirmisher, cavalry trooper, artilleryman, scout, teamster or packer
Second World War: The Soviet Union 3% rifleman, machine gunner, sniper or scout, medic or stretcher-bearer, radio operator or signaller, corporal or sergeant, junior officer, tank crewman
Vietnam War: ARVN chosen, never rolled medic or corpsman
Vietnam War: North Vietnam chosen, never rolled rifleman, point man, scout or sniper, combat engineer or sapper, medic or corpsman
Vietnam War: Viet Cong chosen, never rolled rifleman, point man, scout or sniper, combat engineer or sapper, medic or corpsman, radio operator, squad leader or sergeant, platoon leader
The Falklands to Afghanistan: US 1991 7% combat medic or corpsman, signaller or radio operator, military police or convoy gunner
The Falklands to Afghanistan: Russia 1995 10% combat medic or corpsman
The Falklands to Afghanistan: US 2003-14 11.4% combat medic or corpsman, signaller or radio operator, military police or convoy gunner, team or section leader, platoon leader
The Falklands to Afghanistan: UK 2003-14 8.3% combat medic or corpsman, signaller or radio operator, military police or convoy gunner, team or section leader, platoon leader

For the GM

Pick an era for the fighting you want, not the uniforms. Before the machine gun, battles are decided in the press and the rout, as in the medieval chapters. From 1914 on, men are put down by fire they never see, and what matters is cover, going to ground and the guns. The next chapters cover that.

Guns and fire support

The field map uses the same exchange for every era. What changes after 1865 is the weight of fire, and how men live under it.

Modern infantry

  • Extended order. 3 men to a hex, a few yards apart. Shots at them count half, and they move 8 hexes.
  • Rifles. In a minute a bolt-action rifle fires 10 rounds, a self-loading or assault rifle 15, and a submachine gun or pistol 12. They are rolled as aimed shots at the same rate as a musket's: most rounds are fired at the enemy's line, not at a man.
  • Modern fire puts men down. Against breech-loaders and later weapons, shell and grenades, every serious or critical wound puts a man down, and a light one calls for the stop check (An exchange).
  • Going to ground. On its own move a unit can go to ground in the folds of the ground. Shots at it lose 15% on top of its cover. It cannot move until it gets up, but it still shoots and fights hand to hand.
  • Digging in. A unit with a modern weapon, out of contact, can dig shell scrapes and foxholes: 3 exchanges without moving or firing, and it is dug in where it stands. Dug in, it counts as gone to ground (and hidden, and steadier) while it stays there, but it can get up and move, leaving its holes. In set-up the GM can start units dug in.
  • Hidden men. Men gone to ground, in a trench or a bunker, or in buildings or rubble show little of themselves. Only 10% of the aimed shots at them find a man to aim at (5% of a machine gun's); the rest go at the smoke and the flashes. Dug-in men also hold better: +10 on morale.
  • Machine guns. A machine-gun team serves one gun for every 5 men, and the gun fires while one of its crew is up. It fires 300 rounds a minute, and one in 10 is rolled as an aimed shot.
  • The beaten zone. The cone of fire falls on past its target. The first other unit (friend or foe) within 219 yards (200 m) beyond the target on the line of fire takes 50% as many shots. Woods, rough ground and marsh stop it.
  • Pinned. A unit near a shell burst, or under a machine gun's fire (in its beaten zone too), checks at the end of the exchange: d100 against its Nerve, +10 if gone to ground. On a failure it is pinned for the next exchange: it cannot move, and it shoots at half its rate.

Guns of the black-powder wars

A battery is a unit in battery order, 20 men to a hex. Its men are the crews, 10 to a gun, so as crews fall fewer guns are served.

  • Its fire. Each served gun fires a round an exchange at the nearest enemy in front of it, in sight and with a clear line of fire, out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m) (1,750 yards (1,600 m) for rifled guns). The GM can name another target, split the guns into sections, or choose the shot.
  • Canister. Within 328 yards (300 m) the guns fire canister: 8 chances a round, each likely to hit at short range and less so beyond.
  • Round shot. Beyond that range the guns fire round shot. A ball that strikes a unit ploughs through its ranks, and each man in its path is hit at 40%, so a deep column suffers far more than a line. On firm ground the ball bounds on, and it can strike another unit up to 328 yards (300 m) beyond.
  • Shell. Howitzers fire shell over anything in the way. Its fuse may burst it early, in the air over the men, on the ground, or not at all. Gunners who have found the range cut their fuses better.
  • Wounds. Every man struck by a gun rolls a wound at 80%, with no parry.
  • Rounds. Each gun carries 50 rounds into action. Resupply takes an exchange.
  • Limbering. Changing between limbered and unlimbered takes an exchange. Unlimbered, the guns can only be pushed 2 hexes.
  • Losing the guns. A battery that breaks loses its guns for good.
  • Canister at the charge. Charged in front, a battery gives the first charger one round of canister at point-blank range before the melee.

Fire support

From the First World War on, a side can have batteries off the map: mortars, field guns, heavy howitzers, and tanks or autocannon firing over open sights. Each is a number of tubes with their rounds and crews.

Kind Reach Shells a minute a tube Rounds a tube Lands Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes
Mortars 2.2 miles (3.6 km) 3 60 this exchange 2 hexes 15, 5, 1
Field guns 6.8 miles (11 km) 2 80 next exchange 4 hexes 20, 8, 3, 1
Heavy howitzers 9.0 miles (14.5 km) 1 40 next exchange 5 hexes 30, 12, 5, 2, 1, 0.5
Tanks (direct fire) in sight 2 60 this exchange none 25, 5
Autocannon (direct fire) in sight 3 300 this exchange none 20
  • Calling fire. On its side's move a battery fires on a hex that one of the side's units can see. That means within the weather's sight and the light's, with no woods or smoke between. It can keep firing each exchange until stopped or out of rounds.
  • Where it lands. Each shell scatters by a d6 for the direction and up to the kind's scatter in hexes.
  • What it does. Every man in the burst is struck at the % for his distance from it, ×0.35 if gone to ground and less his cover. A struck man rolls a wound as one hit by shell fragments at 70%. With quick-play, add up each man's chance (men × their % for each burst) for the average and roll once on the spread chart for the men struck.
  • Tree bursts. Over woods, shells burst in the branches. The woods give no cover, the chance is ×1.5, and going to ground only brings it to ×0.7.
  • Smoke spends the same rounds and wounds no one. No one sees or shoots into, out of or through it, and it drifts downwind:
Wind Exchanges it screens after landing Drifts (hexes an exchange)
Calm or light air 3 —
Breeze 2 1
Strong wind 1 2
Gale none: blown away 2
  • Illumination lights the ground round its aim as by day (see Night and the air). It needs no one to see the hex.
  • A fire plan. A creeping barrage lifts its aim 1 to 3 hexes after 1 to 4 exchanges on each line, ahead of an advance kept to the same timetable. A plan can have up to eight legs, each going on the same way or turning.
  • Counter-battery. A battery that has fired is located. Field guns and heavy howitzers can fire on it with no one needing to see it:
  • each shell lands among its guns at 2% (field guns) or 4% (heavy howitzers), knocking out a tube and striking 2 of its crew;
  • at 3 times that chance, it bursts close by and strikes one man.

Counter-battery wears a battery down over a battle rather than ending it. Displacing silences a battery for an exchange or more and leaves it no longer located. - On the map. A battery can stand on a hex of the map instead. From there it reaches only its range, and an enemy unit next to it overruns it.

Trenches and bunkers

A trench gives the men in it cover and hides them, but they fight hand to hand as usual. A bunker shelters its men from shots and shellfire and from blows: no one strikes them, and they strike no one, but they shoot out of it. A tank's shell bursting on it knocks it out at 8%, a heavy howitzer's at 2%.

To take a bunker, a unit next to it storms it with one of three means, once an exchange for each enemy-held bunker across its front, +20 if the bunker's men are pinned:

Means Knocks the bunker out on d100 Men in its hex struck
Grenades 10 or less 40%, as grenade wounds
Satchel charges 25 or less 60%, as grenade wounds
Flamethrowers 40 or less 70%, burned

A man reached by flame is out of the fight with critical burns, and 40% of them are killed outright. A knocked-out bunker is a hex like any other.

For the GM

Under modern fire the question each exchange is who can see whom. Units in the open in close order are cut down. Spread out and gone to ground, they are hard to hit but are pinned half the time. Let the players find a way to move: smoke, a fire plan, a covered approach, or the dark.

Vehicles

On the field map, in wars with machine guns or later, tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and armoured carriers fight as units, one vehicle to a hex. The unit's men are its crews.

Vehicle Crew Move (hexes) Armour Main gun: reach, rounds, hits (close / mid / full) Carries
Tanks 4 12 heavy 1 a vehicle, reach and hits by its fire control (below) —
Infantry fighting vehicles 3 14 light 875 yards (800 m), 2 a vehicle, hits 70/45/20% 7 men
Armoured carriers 3 14 light machine guns only 10 men
Gun tractors and trucks 2 12 soft machine guns only tows 1 gun
Lorries 2 14 soft machine guns only 20 men
Ontos (106 mm recoilless rifles) 3 14 light 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 1 a vehicle, hits 75/50/25% —
  • Moving. Vehicles cross open and high ground at a hex for a hex, and rough ground, slopes and woods for more. They cannot enter marsh, buildings, rubble or water, so in a town they keep to the streets.
  • Their machine guns fire as a machine-gun team's, about one gun to a vehicle.
  • Main guns fire each exchange at the nearest enemy in range, in sight and in front, enemy vehicles first, with a clear line of fire. A tank's gun hits and reaches by its fire control, its war's unless the battlefield gives its own:
Fire control Reach Hits a vehicle (first round, at a standing target) Its wars
Optical sight 1,640 yards (1,500 m) 75% to 219 yards (200 m), 50% to 547 yards (500 m), 25% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 5% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m) WWII, Korea
Stadia reticle 1.2 miles (2 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 35% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 4% to 1.2 miles (2 km) Vietnam
Laser rangefinder 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Late 20th century
Thermal fire control 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Iraq & Afghanistan
  • Armour. Small arms cannot hurt an armoured vehicle, and men armed only with them do not shoot at one. Trucks and gun tractors are soft-skinned: rifles and machine guns shoot at them too, every shot aimed, and each hit knocks one out at the chance below. No one fights a vehicle hand to hand.

Knocking them out

Rocket teams fire a round for every 4 men each exchange, and missile teams one for every 10. Every round is aimed, and range, cover and the weather count as for shots at men. A hit knocks the vehicle out at:

A hit from Heavy armour (tanks) Light armour Soft-skinned (trucks, tractors)
A rocket (RPG, bazooka, recoilless rifle) 15% 50% 80%
A guided missile 60% 90% 95%
A main gun 35% 75% 90%
A rifle or machine-gun bullet — — 5%
  • Where it is hit. A hit into the flank counts ×2, and into the rear ×3, to 100% at most. Which it is depends on where the shooter stands.
  • Composite armour (a battlefield gives it to the M1A1): as heavy armour, but a main gun's round from its front does not knock it out.
  • Morale. A vehicle unit's morale checks count whole vehicles lost, not crewmen hit in vehicles still fighting.
  • Damage short of that. A hit that does not knock the vehicle out strikes the turret at 35%, else the hull.
  • On the turret it puts the main gun out at 40%, and immobilises the vehicle at only 5%.
  • On the hull it immobilises the vehicle at 35%, and puts the gun out at 5%.

Immobilised vehicles can still turn. Their crews can abandon them and leave the fight unhurt. - Shells and bombs bursting in a vehicle's hex knock it out at the kind's own chance: a heavy howitzer's 2%, a fighter-bomber's 15%. Light armour is 3 times as likely to go, soft-skinned vehicles 6 times. - Knocked out. Its crew are out of the fight. Each is struck at 50% and wounded as by shellfire; the rest bail out.

Anti-tank guns

In the Second World War and Korea, a unit can be anti-tank guns: towed guns such as the British 6-pounder, the American 57 mm, the German Pak 38 and 40, the Soviet and North Korean 45 mm and the Japanese 47 mm.

  • Crews. Each gun has 5 men. A gun fires while one of its crew is up, and its crews manhandle it 2 hexes.
  • Fire. Each gun fires 1 round an exchange, as a tank's main gun does. Out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), it hits a vehicle at 70/45/20% (close, mid and full range), and the hit then knocks the vehicle out as a main gun's would. At men, its high explosive bursts as a tank's round does.
  • Towing. Gun tractors and trucks tow a gun each, the crews riding. Hooked up beside them, the guns move with the tractors and do not fire; unhooked, they fire from the next exchange.
  • Rounds. Each gun brings 40 rounds. A gun out of them is resupplied as a battery is: an exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing.
  • Shields. Anti-tank and anti-aircraft guns have shields: small arms fired at them from in front lose 30%. Shields do nothing against shells or fire from the flank or rear. Some machine guns had shields too (a Maxim on a wheeled mount, say), though most did not: in set-up the GM can mark a machine-gun unit shielded, and it gets the same cover.
  • Vulnerable. Otherwise its crews are men: rifles, machine guns and shells strike them, and hand to hand they fight with bayonets.
  • Emplaced. Before the battle the GM can dig in any gun unit (anti-tank guns, anti-aircraft guns, machine guns or a battery). While it stands it counts as gone to ground, −15% and hidden, but it cannot move all battle, though it can turn. A unit that breaks leaves its pits.
  • The enemy commander tows its anti-tank guns forward and unhooks them in reach (see the enemy commander).

Minefields

From 1939, the GM can paint minefields before the battle, marked or hidden. A hidden field shows on the map only once something has gone into it. A unit that moves into minefield hexes sets them off before the exchange's shooting. The ground it crossed is reckoned along the cheapest way it could have gone within its move that crosses the fewest minefield hexes its side knows of, so a known field it went round is not set off; a hidden one on its way is.

Minefield Each man going into a hex struck Each vehicle going into a hex struck
Anti-personnel mines 10% —
Anti-tank mines — 30%
Mixed minefield 8% 25%
  • Men. A man struck rolls a wound as one hit by a mine, at 70%. Mine wounds fall mostly on the feet and legs.
  • Vehicles. A vehicle struck is knocked out at 25% (heavy armour) or 60% (light). Otherwise a track is blown off and it is immobilised.
  • Sappers. In set-up the GM can mark a foot unit as sappers. On its own side's move, before it moves and out of contact, it can start to lay mines of any kind or to lift them. While it works it neither moves nor fires. Moving, turning, breaking or coming into contact stops the work.
  • Laying takes 3 exchanges. Then the row of hexes just ahead of its front, as wide as its front, is a hidden minefield. Hexes where a unit stands are left clear.
  • Lifting takes 2 exchanges. Then the minefield hexes in that row that its side knows of are lifted: a lane.
  • The enemy commander sets its own sappers to work (see the enemy commander).
  • A side knows the mines its own sappers laid: its commander steers round them, and they do not strike its own men.

Riders

Infantry fighting vehicles, carriers and lorries carry men, and tanks carry 6 men on each hull. A foot unit beside them can mount if all its men fit and neither unit is in contact. Riders move with the vehicles. Men in an infantry fighting vehicle shoot through its ports (25% of them) and men on a tank's hull shoot from it (50%), at their own weapon's target; otherwise riders do not fight, shoot or check morale until they dismount beside them. When a carrier is knocked out, each of its riders is struck at 30%, as by shellfire. Lorries are soft-skinned: a rifle or machine-gun hit that does not knock one out strikes a man aboard. Men riding on a tank's hull are in the open: small arms shoot at the tanks for them, and each hit strikes a rider; shells bursting near the tanks strike them as men in the open.

For the GM

Armour is a problem the infantry must solve, not a fight it can win with rifles. Give the side without tanks rockets, anti-tank guns, mines, ground the tanks cannot cross, or the dark.

Night and the air

Fighting in the dark

The light limits how far anyone can see to aim or to call fire, as in Light: on a moonlit night 109 yards (100 m), on a dark night 55 yards (50 m). The weather's own limit still applies, and whichever is shorter counts. The dark also slows a march and turns men round:

Light Movement Losing direction
Daylight — —
Dusk or dawn — —
Moonlit night +1 a hex 10%
Dark night +1 a hex 25%
  • Losing direction. Each unit that moved in the dark may lose its way when its side's move ends. Its chance is the light's, adjusted by its quality: green +12%, regular +5%, veteran −3%. A lost unit ends a point off its line, a hex astray that way (unless that is blocked or touches the enemy), and cannot move next exchange, though it can turn.
  • Muzzle flashes. A unit that fires when the light limits sight to less than 328 yards (300 m) shows where it is. Through the next exchange, the hexes it fired from can be aimed at, and fire called on, from up to 328 yards (300 m) away.
  • Flares. A flare lights the ground within 109 yards (100 m) for 2 exchanges, and illumination rounds from mortars and guns light far more. A lit hex is seen as by day.
  • Night vision. From the 1960s, units can carry devices that see further in the dark. Vehicles carry their war's unless another is chosen: infrared searchlights in Vietnam, thermal sights from the 1980s on. No device sees past the weather's own limit, a sandstorm's included.
  • Infrared beams. A vehicle that fires in the dark by its infrared searchlight lights its target with a beam that enemy infrared sets, Starlight scopes and goggles pick up: through the next exchange, those enemies can aim at the hexes it fired from out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m). A thermal sight does not see the beam.
  • Washed out. A unit standing in a flare's or illumination round's light cannot use a Starlight scope, goggles or infrared set (its men see the dark beyond with their own eyes), and an infrared searchlight there shows no beam. Thermal sights are not washed out.
Device Sees to Aims at worst Through smoke
Starlight scope (1960s-70s) 219 yards (200 m) −15% —
Night-vision goggles (1990s on) 328 yards (300 m) −5% —
Thermal sight (tanks from the 1980s, teams from the 2000s) 656 yards (600 m) as by day yes
Infrared searchlight and sights (tanks, 1950s-70s) 175 yards (160 m) −20% —
  • Fixed lines. Before dark a machine gun can be laid on a fixed line. In the dark, with no target it can see, it fires blind down the line at an enemy within 1 hex of it, at −15%. The enemy commander, holding, lays its machine guns' lines by day or at dusk on the nearest enemy it knows of in reach, or else ahead toward one (or straight ahead) as far as it can reach and see, shifting such a line once onto an enemy that comes into reach off it.
  • The enemy commander knows only what its units see, so at night it waits for the enemy to come close or to fire.

Aircraft

Fighter-bombers and helicopter gunships are called like batteries; each "tube" is an aircraft. Fire can be called only where one of the side's units can see it fall.

Aircraft Comes An aircraft an exchange In all Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes By night
Fighter-bombers (bombs, napalm) 2 exchanges after the call 2 bombs 4 3 hexes 45, 25, 12, 5, 2 no
Helicopter gunships (rockets, guns) at once 4 rocket and gun passes 24 1 hex 20, 6 yes
  • Weather. Aircraft do not fly in fog, storm, heavy snow, blizzard, sandstorm, and fighter-bombers do not fly at night. A mission called then waits until the weather clears.
  • Strafing and napalm. An air attack can be a strafing run or (fighter-bombers, from 1944) a napalm strip, flown along a line the GM chooses. Each pass covers 5 hexes strafing or 3 with napalm.
  • Strafing strikes each man there at 12%, less cover and for going to ground.
  • Napalm strikes at 45% and nothing protects. It puts a man down with critical burns, and kills 35% outright.
  • Marking the target. Smoke laid on the aimed hex before the aircraft arrive halves their scatter, as an air controller does.
  • Ground fire. After each attack run, every aircraft that attacked can be hit.
  • Small arms within 328 yards (300 m) of the aim: 0.5% for each machine gun served there, 1% for each unit with rockets, and 0.2% for every 100 men with other firearms, at most 12% in all.
  • Anti-aircraft guns within 1,094 yards (1,000 m) add 3% for each gun served.

Gunships fly low and slow, so they count it ×2. The whole is at most 35%. Of the aircraft hit, 40% are brought down; the rest are damaged and turn for home. - Air controllers. A unit can be given a forward air controller. When he can see the aim, the attack scatters half as far. Without one, aircraft will not attack within 109 yards (100 m) of their own men; the mission waits until it can.

Landing by air

From Vietnam on, units can come in by helicopter to a landing zone. Each side has so many helicopters: by default X-Ray's 16 Hueys of 5 men each, back for the next load 30 exchanges after they land. At the end of each exchange the free ones fly the lifts in the order called, at most 8 at a zone. The men land on the zone or the nearest spot within 4 hexes, and can move the next exchange.

  • Waved off. No one lands while an enemy unit stands within 2 hexes of the zone.
  • A hot zone. If any enemy unit could shoot at the zone, each man landing is struck at 10% and wounded as by shellfire, and each helicopter is hit at 10%: 20% of those come down on the zone as a wreck, the rest go home damaged. Either way it is lost for the battle.
  • Supplies and extraction. A helicopter can set a supply dump down on a zone, and the helicopters can lift a unit out from near a zone (out of contact; it does not move while it boards). Its men flown out are safe.
  • A downed helicopter gives the men in its hex cover and is slow ground to cross.

For the GM

Night evens the odds against a stronger side, and its fire support and aircraft count for less in the dark. A defender with fixed lines, flares and a plan for illumination can still hold.

A later war: the squad

The medieval chapters followed one retinue. This chapter follows a US Army rifle squad in Vietnam through one night, with the same rules and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the squad.

The squad

The team builder rolls a rifle squad. David Martinez leads it: 3 terms, each a year of the war, so he is 21, with Command 50. Its machine gunner is Dennis Johnson, 2 terms, who fires the gun at 82% but defends at only 15%. Its grenadier is Daniel Garcia, and its medic is Gary Williams, Leechcraft 33. 5 riflemen follow them. Their kit: M1 helmet, nylon flak vest (US Army M1952/M69, 1952-75).

On the field map

The squad: an ambush in the dark

The squad lies in extended order beside a trail on a dark night, gone to ground. No one can see to aim past 55 yards (50 m). Shots at the squad lose 15% for going to ground, and only 10% of the aimed ones find a man to aim at.

An enemy column comes down the trail. When the squad's gun opens fire, its muzzle flashes give it away: the enemy can now aim at its hex from up to 328 yards (300 m). The sergeant calls the company's mortars for illumination. It lands this exchange and lights the trail as by day for 2 exchanges, so his riflemen can aim.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The squad: the gun

An enemy rifleman, a regular, fires his AK at Dennis at 50% and rolls 15: a margin of 35. Against a bullet, an arm takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. Dennis dodges at 15% and rolls 40: no.

The round strikes his upper arm (right), where his vest does not reach. It bleeds 2, pain 2, and the arm is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 45, less 2 steps of pain, gives 25. He rolls 22 and passes: he fights on.

But the machine gun takes both hands. With an arm hurt he cannot fire it, as in Wounds, so he can only defend. At 1 Blood a round, his 19 Blood lasts 19 rounds.

The squad: the grenade

A grenade bursts beside Daniel. The thrower's margin is 25 (he rolled 25). A fragment in the body is serious from a margin of 10, so this is serious, in his chest (left). But his vest, a nylon flak vest (M1952, M69), takes 2 steps off a fragment: it is stopped. Against a rifle round the same vest takes nothing.

The squad: the medic

In a quiet moment Gary crawls to the gun. He binds Dennis's arm at his Leechcraft 33 and rolls 12: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 0. The arm is still hurt (−20% to his attack with it), so another man takes the gun.

At dawn the squad carries him back. His wound goes onto the track as in Recovery.

For the GM

In a later war the heroes are the few men whose names the players know in a fight of hundreds. Keep the field map for the shape of the night and the roller for the moments that matter: a gunner hit, a medic crawling out, a vest that held.
